Where a layer is modelled rather than mapped, `method` says so and `methods` writes the rule out; the app labels it.

keyframes.label: on the eve of contact, c. 1778
keyframes.note: The florescence of the chiefdoms: the windward valleys in loʻi, the leeward field systems at their widest, the lowland forest mostly gone to fields and fire. It also stands for the chiefly eras before it, which had less of everything: the windward irrigated valleys came first, the leeward dryland field systems were laid out and spread after about 1400 and were subdivided and intensified into the 1700s, and fishponds and the great luakini came later still (after Kirch and after Ladefoged and Graves on the Kohala field system; not read for this bake, verify before it reaches a card). The app may fade the dryland part of the cultivation for eras before about 1450 and thin the settlement with it.

keyframes.label: at the Māhele, c. 1848–1855
keyframes.note: The Land Commission Awards of 1846–1855 are a map of where people still lived and farmed, and the 1853 census counts them by island. Seventy-five years of epidemics have emptied much of the land. No forest is baked for this keyframe: nothing maps it, so the app interpolates forest between contact and the end of the kingdom.

keyframes.label: at the end of the kingdom, c. 1896–1900
keyframes.note: Sugar across the plains and lower slopes, loʻi in rice or taro or abandoned, the leeward field systems long empty, cattle and fire pushing the forest line up; Honolulu a city. The 1896 census counts by district; the cane lands are those mapped for 1900.

keyframes.label: now, c. 2010–2020
keyframes.note: For the coda. Mapped from land cover of about 2010, the 2020 agricultural baseline and the 2020 census.

cultivation.rule: The largest of: the Traditional Agriculture zones: loʻi counted at 1, dryland at 0.75, agroforestry at 0.5 of the texel; valley-floor and coastal-plain loʻi read from the pack, counted at 1, because the published zones run on modern soils and stop where those are mapped as urban land or fill (Waikīkī and Honolulu fall outside them): ground on alluvium, lagoon deposits or fill (the geologic map's units, blurred 60 m, times 1.5), below 200–350 m, flatter than 0.06–0.15, no more than 8–25 m above the stream it drains to, where that stream gathers 3–20 million m³ of rain a year from a catchment averaging 1200–2000 mm (each range a smooth ramp; the flow is routed over the pack heights after filling pits); Land Commission Award parcels under 5 ha (kuleana size), as the share of each texel they cover, blurred with a 120 m Gaussian and multiplied by 1.5 (capped at 1) (the parcels claimed in 1848–1855 were lands long in use; how well each model finds them is in baked.calibration); fishpond shore: land within 250 m of the sea and below 6 m where the sea within about 350 m is mostly no deeper than 3 m (a reef flat or sheltered shallows; share 0.5–0.85 ramps 0–1), counted at 0.5: where a loko kuapā could be walled off, not a map of ponds (no statewide inventory exists). Niʻihau and Kahoʻolawe lie outside the agriculture model, so only the pond shore and the few awards there mark them.

settlement.rule: A weight per texel, 0.5 × cultivation blurred at 400 m (people lived among their fields) + 0.35 × a coastal band exp(−distance to sea / 600 m), fading out between 60 and 150 m elevation, times 0.4–1.0 by rain (500–1500 mm) + 0.15 × the kuleana parcels + 0.03 × the rain factor everywhere (people lived thinly on all habitable land); times habitability (none on slopes steeper than about 35°, fading out between 800 and 1,600 m) and 0.3 on lava younger than 50–200 years. Each island’s weights are scaled so that the island holds King’s figure. Kahoʻolawe, which King leaves out, is back-cast from the 80 people the 1832 census counted there by the ratio of King’s 400,000 to the 1832 total of 130,313: 250 people.

sources.title: James King, A Voyage to the Pacific Ocean, vol. III (1784), Book V, pp. 126–128
sources.licence: public domain
sources.note: King’s 1779 estimate island by island, from houses counted around Kealakekua and applied to each coast: 400,000 in all. Estimates for 1778 run from about 200,000 to 1,000,000 (Swanson 2019, Exhibit 1, tabulates them; his own is 683,200), so King’s figures sit inside the range, and every density here scales with whichever total is preferred. King lists no figure for Kahoʻolawe; his 4,000 for "Oreehoua" (Lehua, a bare islet off Niʻihau) is left out.

forest.rule: Closed native forest where the rain allows it (0 at 700 mm a year rising to full at 1,500 mm: the bake’s ramp, set so that Cuddihy and Stone’s line between dry and mesic forest, 1,250 mm as packages/ahupuaa/FOREST.md uses it, falls near its top, since dry forest was mostly open), below the tree line (full to 1,900 m, none by 2,700 m), back from the shore (30–250 m), and on lava old enough to have grown forest (wet ground in 60–300 years, dry ground in 400–2,000). Then cleared as FOREST.md §1 has it from Kirch: below 460 m mostly farmed or burned (0.12 kept, rising to 0.5 where the nearest field is 1.5–6 km away), essentially untouched above 760 m, a ramp between; and never on cultivated ground. Wherever native forest still stands today (CAH) on ground no lava has covered since 1778, it stood then too, so the layer is never less than that. Niʻihau has no rain grid and is taken as dry.

zoning.rule: A texel takes the class covering most of its area: it is split into s × s samples about 8 m apart (19 m on Hawaiʻi, whose texels are 151 m), each sample takes the class of the polygon over its centre, and the commonest class among the samples wins, provided classed samples cover at least 25% of the texel; otherwise, and wherever the pack is sea, the value is 0. Roads, streams, drainage and land a county marks as not zoned count as no class, so a road through a town takes the town’s class. A pack holds the slivers of neighbours in its box; they are classed by their own county’s layer or left 0.

crops.about: What grows on each land texel at each era keyframe: per island pack and keyframe, an 8-bit greyscale PNG of class numbers with exactly the bounds and size of its pack in ../manifest.json (texel registration as DATA.md has it), 0 over sea. Class numbers are categories: sample them nearest, never filtered, and take the nearest keyframe for an era (eras), never a blend of bytes. A texel with cultivation above 0 and class 0 is drawn as the era’s default; pasture and lawn may stand where the cultivation mask is 0, and so may two classes the cultivation masks leave out (uncultivated). Where a class is modelled rather than mapped, methods says so and writes the rule out.

classes.0: nothing, or cultivation of no known kind
classes.2: dryland fields: sweet potato, dry taro, the leeward field systems
classes.3: rice, in old loʻi and marsh

uncultivated.4: at mahele only: the cultivation mask has no cane, so the class alone marks the plantations
uncultivated.7: at kingdom only: the cultivation mask leaves coffee out, so the class alone marks it

contact.rule: Where the contact cultivation mask (layers/<island>/contact-cultivation.png) is above 0, the term of its rule that is largest there names the field: the loʻi rule (the Kurashima–Kirch loʻi zones and the valley-floor and coastal-plain rule) gives loʻi (1); the dryland and agroforestry zones give dryland (2); the kuleana parcels give loʻi where the loʻi rule reaches 0.25 there and dryland elsewhere; the fishpond shore gives 0 (a pond’s shore, no crop: the app draws its default). Nothing else grows at contact: classes 1, 2 and 0 only.
contact.limits: As good as the cultivation model beneath it (RESEARCH §9): the dryland zones are the published model of the leeward field systems, not their surveyed footprints; East Hawaiʻi and windward East Maui are thin; the loʻi/dryland line follows which term of the model is largest, not a field survey.

mahele.rule: Where the mahele cultivation mask (layers/<island>/mahele-cultivation.png) is above 0, the term of its rule that is largest there names the field: the loʻi rule (the Kurashima–Kirch loʻi zones and the valley-floor and coastal-plain rule) gives loʻi (1); the dryland and agroforestry zones give dryland (2); the kuleana parcels give loʻi where the loʻi rule reaches 0.25 there and dryland elsewhere; the fishpond shore gives 0 (a pond’s shore, no crop: the app draws its default), the abandonment since contact being already in the mask’s lower weights. Cane (4): each plantation grinding by 1853 (Kōloa, Līhuʻe, Hāna, Lāhainā) drawn as 300 acres (no acreage for 1853 was found for any of them, so every one takes this nominal figure) of the land nearest its mill below 300 m and flatter than 15%, not loʻi, land that was cane in 1900 counting as 2 times nearer; the 1853 cultivation mask has no cane, so these texels may be 0 in it. Pasture (6): the ranches by 1853 (Parker, at Waimea, 1847; Kualoa (Judd), 1850; Torbertsville (ʻUlupalakua), 1841), whose grazed land is not known, only their bounds (the ahupuaʻa named in record.ranches1853), so the lower, drier part of the bounds: below 2,000 m, with 400–2,000 mm of rain a year (neither the bare leeward coast nor the wet forest belt), outside the keyframe’s forest (under 50%) and fields (cultivation under 25%). No rice: it was started in 1858 (record.leftOut).
mahele.limits: The plantations are discs of a nominal size around their towns; Hilo’s mills and the East Maui plantation are left out (record.leftOut says why). Pasture is three ranches; the wild cattle of the Waimea plains and Mauna Kea, the herds kept across every island, are not drawn.

kingdom.rule: Mapped: cane (4) and pineapple (5) where the 1900 cane and pineapple lands are the largest term of the kingdom cultivation mask. Modelled: elsewhere, where the kingdom cultivation mask (layers/<island>/kingdom-cultivation.png) is above 0, the term of its rule that is largest there names the field: the loʻi rule (the Kurashima–Kirch loʻi zones and the valley-floor and coastal-plain rule) gives loʻi (1); the dryland and agroforestry zones give dryland (2); the kuleana parcels give loʻi where the loʻi rule reaches 0.25 there and dryland elsewhere; the fishpond shore gives 0 (a pond’s shore, no crop: the app draws its default). Rice (3): in each district an opened source puts rice in (record.rice1896), the cultivated texels classed loʻi, dryland or none that lie below 15 m and flatter than 6%, on loʻi ground (the loʻi rule at 0.25 or more) or wet ground (alluvium, lagoon deposits or fill at 0.5 or more): “the lowest flats found at the outlets of valleys and close on the sea”; where the 1892 figure of a district is known (Hanalei and Waiʻoli 750 acres, Mokulēʻia 738, Kailua and Waimānalo 400) up to that figure, the old loʻi first (the strongest loʻi rule, then the lowest ground: the rice took over abandoned taro land first), and there rice may take land that was cane by 1900. Coffee (7): in Kona, the land that was at least 50% coffee (O-5) in 1978–80, read back; at Olaʻa, 4,093.5 acres (the 1897 count of coffee land a year old or more) of the land between 1,500 and 2,500 feet nearest the Volcano Road; the kingdom cultivation mask leaves coffee out, so these texels may be 0 in it. Pasture (6): in the bounds of each ranch of the Annual’s list (record.ranches1896: the moku of its listed district), the land that was at least 50% grazing (A-1) in 1978–80, read back, where in 1896 it was under 25% cultivated and under 50% forest and not cane, pineapple, rice or coffee; on Lānaʻi, Niʻihau and Kahoʻolawe, whole-island sheep and cattle ranges the 1978–80 map cannot give back (it leaves out Niʻihau and Kahoʻolawe, and Lānaʻi was pineapple by then), all the land below 2,000 m that is neither forest nor field.
kingdom.limits: Cane and pineapple are of 1900, four years on. Kahoʻolawe’s range is the KIRC timeline’s “first of many ranch leases” from 1858 and its late-1890s stock, not a map. Rice is placed by rule inside districts, not mapped: no map of the rice fields of the 1890s was found, and the 1927 sheets show what was left after annexation turned rice land to cane (none at Mokulēʻia or Waikīkī by then). Its districts are the ones a source names; Maui, Hawaiʻi Island and Koʻolauloa grew rice too, unplaced. Where no figure caps a district (Waikīkī, the ʻEwa shore, Kāneʻohe and the rest) all the land on the rule is rice, which likely overstates Oʻahu, whose lowlands also held taro, ponds and pasture. Pasture is the grazing of 1978–80 read back into the 1890s ranches’ districts: right where the ranches kept their land, wrong where grazing spread after 1896 (cleared forest) or gave way (pineapple, towns). Kona’s coffee is the coffee of 1980 read back, more than the 1,150 acres estimated for 1892 and probably less than the 1890s boom planted.

now.rule: The 2020 agricultural baseline: each texel takes the group of categories covering most of it (mapping.now) when the groups together cover 25% of it or the now cultivation mask is above 0: taro loʻi (1); pineapple (5); orchard, coffee, macadamia, fruit, flowers, seed and diversified crops (7); pasture and dairy (6). No cane: the last plantation closed in 2016, and the 14 acres the layer still calls Sugar count as 7. Lawn (8): where no crop is, the CAH land cover’s developed open space covers 50% of the texel and either the county zones it parks and open space (now-zoning.png class 12) or a golf course lies within 600 m (scaled by the square root of its holes over 18) of the point the State layer gives it.
now.limits: The baseline maps commercial agriculture only (household gardens and small loʻi are not in it). The lawns need two sources to agree, so a park the zoning misses or turf the land cover of about 2010 calls something else is not lawn; the golf courses are points, so a course’s lawn is the open space near its point. Kahoʻolawe and Niʻihau have no zoning and no golf, so no lawn.
